::: {#def-positional-invariance .theorem}
## Positional invariance

The value of a component function is unchanged by a re-ordering of network values together with the same re-ordering of network weights. For all $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{X}' \in \{0,1\}^n$ and every permutation matrix $\mathbf M$,

$$
\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{X}'_{\mathcal{N}_j}, \quad \Psi_{i,\mathcal{N}_i} = \mathbf{M}\Psi_{j,\mathcal{N}_j} \Rightarrow g_{ti}(\mathbf{X}) = g_{tj}(\mathbf{X}').
$$

An exposure mapping is positionally invariant with respect to a graph set $\mathcal H = \{\mathscr{G}_t\}_{t \in [1:K]}$ if it is [separable](#def-separability) and each component function is positionally invariant with respect to an element of $\mathcal H$. Two nodes in the same local configuration are summarized the same way, whoever they are and wherever they sit.

This is what makes the notation of the identification formulas legitimate. Without it there are $n$ separate component functions $g_{t1},\dots,g_{tn}$, one per unit; positional invariance collapses them into a single function of the values and the node's position, so that one $g_Y(\mathbf L, \Psi_i)$ can stand for every $i$.
:::
